source.version: Journal article published online 28 May 2026, Artificial Intelligence and Applications, Vol. 00(00); complete 22-page PDF
source.title_on_document: Future AI Systems: Human–AI Collaborative Teams Outperform Human-Only Teams in Design Ideation

paper_design_summary: A laboratory experiment randomly placed senior undergraduates and beginning graduate students in human-human (HH) or human-AI (HAI) teams to sketch solutions for getting a toddler into bed and transporting a computer on campus. The AI collaborator was an AutoDraw-based Disruptive Interjector: although called generative, its implementation is described as classifying sketches and retrieving suggestions from an existing image library (pp. 2, 5-7, Sections 2.1 and 3.1-3.3). Trained research assistants rated sketches for novelty and usefulness, and the paper compared idea counts and ratings between conditions (pp. 8, 10, Sections 4.1-4.6).

studies.label: Human-human versus human-AI collaborative design sketching

assignment.what_was_assigned: Participants were placed in an HH team with another human or an HAI team with the AI collaborator; the AI suggestion feature was disabled for HH teams.
assignment.quote: They were randomly placed in either an HH team or an HAI team, as illustrated in Figure 5.
assignment.locator: p. 6, Section 3.2 (Study setup); p. 7, Section 3.3 (condition implementation)

arms.name: Human-human (HH)
arms.description: Two humans collaborated using the tablet sketching application with the AI suggestion feature disabled (p. 1, Abstract; p. 7, Sections 3.2-3.3 and Table 3). Arm-specific randomized and analyzed people counts are not explicitly reported; team counts are not entered as people counts.

arms.name: Human-AI (HAI)
arms.description: A human collaborated with the Disruptive Interjector, receiving image suggestions while sketching (p. 1, Abstract; p. 5, Section 3.1; p. 7, Table 3). Coded other_aid because the described implementation retrieves existing images; the paper also calls it generative. Arm-specific randomized and analyzed people counts are not explicitly reported.

participants.exclusions: After assignment, sketches from two HAI teams were set aside because they combined multiple ideas on one screen. A further team was excluded because both members knew each other, frequently worked on problem-solving together, and had expert-level design experience (pp. 8 and 10, Section 4.2; p. 17, Section 6.3). Duplicate screenshots and test marks were also excluded (p. 8, Section 4). Common/not-novel and nonsensical/not-useful sketches were set aside from the main rated subset (pp. 8 and 10, Sections 4.2-4.3; p. 14, Section 4.7). The paper reports 263 sketches initially (p. 8, Section 3.4), 216 sketches after removing the two categories of excluded teams (p. 17, Section 6.3 and Table 8), and 122 sketches from 31 participants remaining after grouping (p. 15, Section 5), compared with 35 participants assigned (p. 6, Section 3.2). These are different analysis sets; sketch counts are not people counts. The paper does not explicitly report arm-specific participant exclusions.
participants.who: Senior undergraduates and beginning graduate students in cross-disciplinary programs including engineering and design, familiar with sketching to express ideas; recruited by email and studied in dedicated university or university-approved research facilities.
participants.quote: 122 sketches from 31 participants remained for evaluation after the first round of grouping by the trained research assistants.
participants.locator: p. 6, Section 3.2 (35 participants and random placement); p. 7, Section 3.3 (recruitment and setting); p. 15, Section 5 (31 participants retained for evaluation)

ai_tool.name_model: Disruptive Interjector using Google AutoDraw; described implementation incorporates a pretrained ResNet-50 image classifier
ai_tool.how_used: Observed tablet sketches in real time, matched them to images in a curated library, and displayed matching images as suggestions. Participants could accept, reject, combine, or use suggestions as inspiration. The author calls the system generative, but the technical description documents image classification and retrieval rather than generation of new images (pp. 2, 4-6, Sections 2.1, 2.4 and 3.1; p. 7, Table 3).

task.description: Sketch as many solutions as possible to getting a toddler into bed, then transporting a computer on campus; save each sketch and select a final concept for each task (p. 7, Sections 3.2-3.3 and Table 3).
task.duration: Two consecutive tasks, approximately 7 min each (p. 7, Sections 3.2-3.3 and Table 3).

outcomes.name: Idea quality based on novelty and usefulness: reported significance tests
outcomes.question: with_ai
outcomes.measure_detail: Two trained research assistants independently rated novelty and usefulness as separate characteristics (p. 7, Section 3.2; p. 8, Section 4.1). Each uses scores 1 to 4, with an additional zero for ideas judged not novel or not useful, respectively (p. 10, Section 4.3). The retained 122 sketches generated 488 ratings across two aspects and two raters (p. 12, Section 4.6); neither count is a count of people. Table 6 does not specify which score or aggregation entered the tests, so the analysis unit remains unconfirmed (p. 15, Section 4.8). The sketches were produced during the tasks with the retrieval aid available to HAI teams and disabled for HH teams (p. 7, Sections 3.2-3.3; p. 10, Section 4.5).

contrasts.reported: HAI versus HH, independent-samples tests using equal_var=False: All ideas (263), t-test statistic = 3.814, p-value = 0.00014; Highly rated (122), t-test statistic = 2.773, p-value = 0.00729. The paper does not specify precisely which score or aggregation entered these tests, so the analysis unit is unconfirmed. Table 6 labels the values t-test statistics, while the following prose calls them means.
contrasts.locator: p. 10, Section 4.3 (novelty and usefulness rated by trained assistants); p. 15, Section 4.8 and Table 6 (tests)

outcomes.name: Ideas receiving the highest novelty rating
outcomes.question: with_ai
outcomes.measure_detail: Two trained research assistants independently rated novelty and usefulness separately (p. 7, Section 3.2; p. 8, Section 4.1). Novelty anchors were 1 = somewhat similar to other ideas, 2 = neither similar nor different, 3 = somewhat different, and 4 = very different; common ideas received zero. Usefulness also used scores 1 to 4, with zero for not-useful/nonsensical ideas (p. 10, Section 4.3). The retained 122 sketches yielded 488 ratings across both aspects and both raters (p. 12, Section 4.6); these are output and rating counts, not people. The reported novelty thresholds are at least one rating of 4 and ratings of 4 from both raters (p. 16, Section 5 and Table 7); repeated sketch IDs and the different cutoff in Section 6.3 prevent treating the counts as verified distinct ideas. The sketches were produced during the tasks with the retrieval aid available to HAI teams and disabled for HH teams (p. 7, Sections 3.2-3.3; p. 10, Section 4.5).

contrasts.reported: The text reports 17 HAI ideas versus 5 HH ideas receiving a 4 from at least one rater, and 8 HAI versus 2 HH ideas receiving a 4 from both raters. These are the printed counts: Table 7 contains repeated sketch IDs, so they should not be treated as verified counts of distinct ideas. Section 6.3 also reuses the 17 versus 5 counts with a different stated cutoff (average rating 4.0 or 3.5).
contrasts.locator: p. 10, Section 4.3 (rating scale); p. 16, Table 7 and Section 5 (counts and repeated entries); p. 17, Section 6.3 (different cutoff)

contrasts.reported: HAI teams: mean = 11.9, standard deviation = 5.8; HH teams: mean = 8.5, standard deviation = 3.2. Section 4.5 reports 21 teams in total. Table 5 supplies the arm means and SDs but no arm-specific n; the sample count recorded here is the total number of teams, not people.

outcomes.name: Usefulness of sketches: separate ratings
outcomes.question: with_ai
outcomes.measure_detail: Two trained evaluators independently rated how well each sketch could solve the assigned task (p. 7, Section 3.2; p. 10, Section 4.3). Usefulness anchors were 1 = slightly useful, 2 = moderately useful, 3 = very useful, and 4 = extremely useful; nonsensical/not-useful sketches received zero (p. 10, Section 4.3). Section 5 reports sketches, whereas Section 6.3/Table 8 reports rating occurrences from a different analysis set; no single analysis unit or denominator is confirmed for these summaries. The sketches were produced during the tasks with the retrieval aid available to HAI teams and disabled for HH teams (p. 7, Sections 3.2-3.3; p. 10, Section 4.5).

contrasts.reported: Section 5 reports 4 sketches receiving a usefulness rating of 4; none received a novelty rating of 3 or 4. Section 6.3 and Table 8 instead report that usefulness received a rating of 4 on 9 occasions (2%) among 216 evaluated sketches after the specified team exclusions. The paper does not reconcile these counts: the first counts sketches and the second counts rating occurrences. No separate arm mean, arm-specific usefulness contrast, or effect estimate is reported; the direction is therefore unconfirmed.
contrasts.locator: p. 7, Section 3.2 (independent evaluators); p. 10, Section 4.3 (scale); p. 16, Section 5 (4 sketches); p. 17, Section 6.3 and Table 8 (9 rating occurrences, 2%, 216 sketches)

outcomes.name: Variety of idea categories represented within each team
outcomes.question: with_ai
outcomes.measure_detail: The raters grouped similar ideas, and variety was defined as the number of those groups represented within each team's ideas (p. 10, continuation of Section 4.2 and Section 4.5, item 6). This is within-team category breadth, coded flexibility; it does not measure similarity across different people. The sketches were produced during the tasks with the retrieval aid available to HAI teams and disabled for HH teams (p. 7, Sections 3.2-3.3; p. 10, Section 4.5).

contrasts.reported: No numerical HH-versus-HAI result is reported for the number of categories represented within teams. The continuation of Section 4.2 describes 16 groups: 9 for the toddler task and 7 for the computer task. Section 4.5, item 6, instead describes 9 groups for the first task and 6 for the second. The paper does not reconcile this category-count discrepancy; no score, effect, direction, or number of analyzed teams for this outcome is inferred.
contrasts.locator: p. 10, continuation of Section 4.2 (16 groups: 9 and 7); p. 10, Section 4.5, item 6 (9 and 6)

eligibility.reason: Random assignment itself is explicit: 35 participants were randomly placed in HH or HAI teams (p. 6, Section 3.2), so assignment.randomized is yes. Criterion 1 is unclear specifically as to in-scope generative-AI assistance: the author calls the tool generative (pp. 4-5, Section 2.4), but its implementation matches sketches to existing images and retrieves suggestions from a library using an image classifier (p. 2, Section 2.1; pp. 5-6, Section 3.1), which does not establish generative assistance under the codebook. Independently, only 31 people remained for the main evaluation (p. 15, Section 5), below the 50-person threshold; even the initial 35 is below it. Novelty and usefulness were scored on participants' sketches by trained evaluators (p. 7, Section 3.2; p. 10, Section 4.3), satisfying criterion 3. This is a small randomized experiment, not an observational or AI-versus-human-output context study.

one_line_finding: In a randomized study with 31 participants retained for evaluation (p. 15, Section 5), HAI teams averaged 11.9 sketches (SD 5.8) versus 8.5 (SD 3.2) for HH teams (p. 12, Table 5).
